In Ontario, during a Real Estate purchase, a Writ of Execution is has been discovered for a debtor owing about $500,000 to Bank of Montreal that has a similar name to the me. He happens to have the same surname, and one forename. The other parts of the names are different. We are factually different people, and I do not know this individual. Our lawyer says we need to get a clearance letter to satisfy the lender/title insurer and close on time. The creditor's law firm has asked for about $480 to produce the letter. Attempts by our lawyer to get them to lower their price went unanswered. The closing date is on August 26, 2026 We will have to pay the absurdly high $480 rather than risk the transaction. I want to persue the creditor's law firm and seek reimbursement after the fact on principle. Is that realistic and how would I go about doing that?

Yes, reimbursement is possible in theory, but a standalone claim for the $480 is unlikely to be commercially realistic unless the law firm acted improperly or demanded an amount that was clearly unjustified. The immediate priority should be closing on August 26, 2026, while preserving your position and creating a paper trail.

Why the letter may be required

Ontario land-registration practice distinguishes between an ordinary affidavit and creditor confirmation. For a writ of $50,000 or more, written acknowledgment from the judgment creditor or its solicitor that the registered owner is not the judgment debtor may be used to clear the issue. The Ontario guidance also says that a solicitor for the registered owner may make an unequivocal statement that their client is not the same person, although your lender or title insurer may still insist on creditor confirmation.ontario+1

The writ is not automatically enforceable against your property merely because someone has a similar name. Ontario guidance states that an execution search is against the exact registered-owner name, and a writ filed under a different name has no effect against that owner. However, the title insurer and lender may reasonably require documentary comfort before advancing funds.ontario

How realistic is recovery?

Your prospects depend heavily on what the $480 represents:

SituationLikely position
The firm is charging a disclosed administrative/legal fee for voluntarily investigating and issuing a clearance letterRecovery is difficult; there may be no general duty to provide the service for free.
The writ was filed against the wrong person because of the creditor’s negligent identificationA claim may be arguable, but you would need to establish negligence, causation, and actual loss.
The firm refuses to correct an obvious error, provides misleading information, or deliberately uses the title problem to extract moneyYour position becomes materially stronger, particularly if you have clear identity documents and evidence of unreasonable conduct.
The fee is actually a sheriff, court, registration, or other statutory chargeRecovery would generally be unlikely unless the charge was improperly imposed. Ontario publishes separate court and enforcement fees for writ-related steps. ontario
The fee is simply your lawyer’s charge for dealing with the issueThat should be assessed separately from the creditor’s law firm’s fee.

A court would not necessarily award the fee merely because the charge feels excessive. You would generally need to show that the creditor or its lawyers caused a reasonably foreseeable loss through wrongful or negligent conduct, and that paying the fee was reasonably necessary to avoid a larger loss.

What to do before closing

Ask your lawyer to send a formal letter immediately—preferably marked “without prejudice” where appropriate—that:

  • confirms in writing that you are not the judgment debtor;

  • provides enough identifying information to distinguish you, without disclosing unnecessary personal information;

  • demands the letter by a fixed deadline;

  • requests an itemized explanation of the $480, including taxes, disbursements, and the work allegedly required;

  • states that payment is made under protest and solely to avoid a failed or delayed closing;

  • expressly reserves all rights to seek reimbursement, damages, interest, and costs; and

  • asks whether the firm will issue the letter without charge or hold the fee in trust pending resolution.

Do not personally contact the bank or opposing law firm in a way that could create confusion. Have your lawyer make the communication and ensure the letter uses the exact legal names and property details required by the lender and title insurer.

Also ask your lawyer whether the lender/title insurer would accept an unequivocal solicitor’s statement from your lawyer instead. Ontario’s writ guidance recognizes that route, although the particular lender or insurer may impose stricter underwriting requirements.files.ontario

Preserve the evidence

Keep:

  • the title and writ search;

  • the writ details and judgment-debtor name;

  • all correspondence and unanswered requests;

  • the $480 demand and any invoice;

  • proof of payment;

  • your lawyer’s time records and extra fees;

  • evidence of the closing deadline;

  • proof that the payment was necessary to obtain financing or title insurance; and

  • documents showing the differences between you and the actual debtor.

Your lawyer should also obtain a receipt that describes the payment as a fee for investigating and issuing a mistaken-identity clearance, rather than as payment of the debtor’s judgment.

Post-closing options

Negotiation first

After closing, send a structured demand to the creditor’s law firm and copy the bank’s legal or complaints department. Explain that:

  1. you were not the debtor;

  2. their writ created a title/financing impediment;

  3. the $480 was paid under protest;

  4. the payment was reasonably necessary to protect the transaction; and

  5. you seek reimbursement within a specified period.

Request the firm’s legal basis for the fee and an itemized account. A professional complaint to the firm’s managing partner may be more effective than immediately starting litigation.

Complaint about the lawyers

You can complain to the Law Society of Ontario if you believe the lawyers acted dishonestly, improperly, or unprofessionally. However, the Law Society does not set ordinary legal fees and generally cannot order a lawyer to reimburse you simply because a fee seems too high.lso+1

The LSO Compensation Fund is generally not the appropriate remedy here: it is directed primarily at losses caused by lawyer or paralegal dishonesty, not ordinary fee disputes or compensation for a creditor’s mistaken title problem.lso

Civil claim

A civil claim could potentially allege negligence, negligent misrepresentation, interference with economic interests, or another recognized cause of action, depending on the evidence and the precise role of the creditor and its lawyers. You should obtain independent advice from a litigation lawyer who does not represent you on the purchase, because your conveyancing lawyer may have a conflict or may not handle this type of claim.

For only $480, litigation is usually uneconomic: the filing fee, service, legal research, and your time could exceed the amount sought. The better strategy is often a carefully prepared demand followed by a complaint to the bank and firm, unless the incident caused additional losses such as a failed closing, bridge-financing costs, penalties, or substantial extra legal fees.

Important practical point

Before paying, ask your lawyer to confirm whether the $480 is being paid to the creditor’s law firm, to the sheriff, or through your own lawyer as part of a broader title-insurance process. Those are legally and practically different situations. Also ask whether your lawyer can obtain a written undertaking that the firm will refund the fee if the creditor later confirms that the writ was misidentified.

This is general Ontario information, not a substitute for advice from a litigation lawyer. Given the closing date, ask your conveyancing lawyer today for a written assessment of whether the fee is unavoidable and whether an unequivocal solicitor’s statement is acceptable to the lender or title insurer.
